passage: I'm Varun, and I want to write about Nilesh. In the spelling test before Diwali, I saw him look at the paper next to him and copy a word. After that, everything he did looked bad to me. When he drew a tiger for the class wall, I told everyone it looked like a cat. When he offered me his extra eraser, I said no, as if it was dirty. When he laughed, I thought he was laughing at someone. Last week our art teacher hung his tiger in the corridor and said it had the best stripes she had seen all year. I stood and looked at it properly for the first time. It was good. I felt strange. He copied one word. That didn't make his tiger bad.

qa.q: What did Nilesh draw for the class wall?
qa.a: He drew a tiger for the class wall.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling when looking at the tiger properly for the first time?
qa.a: Varun felt strange and a little ashamed, seeing that the drawing was good and that one copied word had coloured everything.

qa.q: What could Varun try the next time one bad act makes someone seem all bad?
qa.a: Varun could judge each thing on its own, like looking at the drawing itself, instead of letting the copied word decide.

qa.q: How might Nilesh have felt when Varun refused his eraser?
qa.a: Nilesh probably felt hurt and confused, since he was only trying to be friendly.

grounding: A child looks back on how seeing a classmate copy once made everything about him, even his drawing and kindness, seem bad.

passage:
Class 4 observation, week of 12 August.
Sunaina has refused to be in Kunal's group three times this week. When he offered to share his crayons, she pushed them back. In music she told her friends his singing was "the worst." When I asked her why, she said, "He looked at the answer card in the maths quiz. He's a cheater. Everything he does is bad." I did see Kunal peek that day, and I spoke to him about it privately at the time. Today I sat with Sunaina and asked her to tell me one thing Kunal does well. It took a while. Then: "He helps the little ones tie their shoes." Next step: I will pair them for the garden job on Monday and watch how it goes.

qa.q: What did Sunaina say about Kunal's singing?
qa.a: She told her friends his singing was "the worst."

qa.q: Why does Sunaina feel so sure everything about Kunal is bad?
qa.a: Seeing him peek at the answer card left her angry and disgusted, and that one act now feels to her like the whole truth about him.

qa.q: What did the teacher do to loosen Sunaina's view?
qa.a: The teacher asked her to name one thing Kunal does well and planned to pair them for the garden job, so she can see more of him.

qa.q: What is it like for Kunal to be shut out all week?
qa.a: Kunal is probably hurt and lonely, pushed away even when he offers crayons, long after his mistake was dealt with.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a child who saw a classmate peek at answers deciding his singing, sharing and everything else are bad too.

passage:
Dear diary, Sunday.
Today Sumit came to our building's cricket match and everyone picked him first. I didn't clap. On Friday, in the drawing competition, I saw him trace a peacock from a book hidden under his paper. So now I know he is a cheater. His jokes are not funny. His new bicycle is ugly. And when he gave me back my lost hair clip at the gate, I thought he was just showing off. But then Ammi said, "He walked all the way back to the park to find it for you." I didn't know what to say. Maybe tracing is bad but finding the clip is good? It's confusing. I'm writing it here so I can think.
Afreen

qa.q: What did Afreen see Sumit do in the drawing competition?
qa.a: Afreen saw him trace a peacock from a book hidden under his paper.

qa.q: Why did Afreen think Sumit was showing off with the hair clip?
qa.a: Afreen felt so angry about the tracing that even his kindness seemed suspicious; one wrong act had soured everything.

qa.q: What could help Afreen think about Sumit more fairly?
qa.a: Afreen could look at each act on its own, the tracing as wrong and finding the clip as kind, instead of letting one act decide all.

qa.q: How does Ammi see Sumit's return of the clip?
qa.a: Ammi sees it as a kind effort, since he walked all the way back to the park to find it.

grounding: A child's diary shows how seeing a classmate trace a drawing makes his jokes, bicycle and even his kindness seem bad.

passage: In Class 10C of the Andheri school, the physics teacher had a name for Ujjwal: "our sleeping beauty." It started in June, when he dozed off once after a late night helping at his uncle's shop. Since then, nothing he did seemed to count. On Tuesday he handed in his lab record two days early, every diagram labelled in blue ink. The teacher flipped through it and said, "Who helped you, Ujjwal?" That same afternoon he forgot his ID card, and the teacher said, loud enough for the whole row, "Of course. Some things never change." Vasudha, who sat next to him, saw him close the record slowly and stare at the desk. "Your diagrams were better than mine," she whispered. He shrugged. "Doesn't matter. I'm the lazy one." That evening he didn't start the next chapter.

qa.q: When did Ujjwal hand in his lab record?
qa.a: He handed it in two days early, on Tuesday.

qa.q: What does Ujjwal's "I'm the lazy one" suggest he is feeling?
qa.a: He feels defeated and hurt, as if the label has become who he is, so effort no longer seems worth it.

qa.q: How could a teacher support Ujjwal instead?
qa.a: The teacher could praise the early, careful lab record on its own merits and handle the ID card quietly, without tying both to an old label.

qa.q: How does Vasudha see Ujjwal's work?
qa.a: Vasudha sees it clearly as good, saying his diagrams were better than hers, and notices how the label is wearing him down.

grounding: Shows a teenager labelled lazy by a teacher whose early, careful work is doubted while a small slip is loudly noticed.

passage:
"Sahil, why is your name on the board again?"
"The fan switch broke. Ma'am saw me standing near it, so obviously it was me."
"Was it?"
"No! It was already hanging loose. But I'm 'the naughty boy', Sunaina. Since Class 7."
"Because of the water balloon thing?"
"One water balloon. Two years ago."
"But you won the essay prize last week."
"She read it out and said, 'Surprising.' That's it. Then when I dropped my compass, she said, 'Typical.'"
"That's not fair."
"Whatever. Why try? She's already decided."
"Don't say that. Come with me to the class teacher at lunch. I'll tell her the switch was loose. I saw it on Monday."
"You'd do that?"
"Yes. And you keep writing essays."

qa.q: What did the teacher say when reading out Sahil's essay?
qa.a: She read it out and said, 'Surprising.'

qa.q: Why does Sahil say "Why try?"
qa.a: He feels hopeless and resentful, since his good work gets a shrug while every small slip is called typical of him.

qa.q: What does Sunaina offer to do, and why might it help?
qa.a: She offers to go with him to the class teacher and say the switch was already loose, giving an adult a fair account beyond the label.

qa.q: What would change if the teacher saw Sahil without the old label?
qa.a: The essay prize would be praised as real achievement and the broken switch would be checked, not blamed on him.

grounding: Shows a teenager labelled naughty by a teacher, whose essay prize is shrugged off while every slip is called typical.

passage: Looking back at Class 9, I think one word did more damage than any mark. In the first week I forgot my homework twice, and Salma ma'am started calling me "careless Pankaj, our dreamy boy." After that it followed me everywhere. When I built a working water filter for the science fair, she asked which cousin had made it. When I scored the second-highest in the unit test, she said the paper must have been easy. But when I came in two minutes late after the bus broke down, it went into my diary for my parents to sign. By December I had stopped raising my hand. What was the point? Only in Class 10, with a new teacher who had never heard the word, did I start answering again. I was still the same boy.

qa.q: What did Pankaj build for the science fair?
qa.a: A working water filter.

qa.q: Why had Pankaj stopped raising his hand by December?
qa.a: He felt discouraged and unseen, because his good work was doubted while every small slip was recorded.

qa.q: What does the Class 10 change suggest a teacher could do?
qa.a: Come to each student fresh and judge the work in front of them, since without the label Pankaj started answering again.

qa.q: How might Salma ma'am have seen Pankaj's good test score?
qa.a: Through the careless label she read it as an easy paper rather than his effort, so the success didn't change her view.

grounding: A teenager looks back on being labelled careless by a teacher, so his real work was doubted while small slips were always recorded.

passage: You want to know why Vishal isn't on the slides? Okay, honestly, it's like this. I'm Kamal, I'm the group lead, right? First week, Vishal sent his literature summary a day late. One day, but the whole draft got held up. So I thought, fine, he's useless, I'll just do his part. Since then I haven't given him a single task. Not the survey, not the slides, nothing. I didn't even open his messages, I just assumed they were excuses. Yesterday our professor asked who built the data sheet, and Vishal said, very quietly, that he had offered to twice and I'd said no. And he was right. He was late once. I made him invisible for a month. I still don't know what to say to him.

qa.q: What did Vishal send a day late in the first week?
qa.a: His literature summary.

qa.q: How was Kamal feeling after the professor's question?
qa.a: Kamal seems embarrassed and guilty, seeing that one late summary had been turned into a month of shutting Vishal out.

qa.q: What could Kamal do now to repair things?
qa.a: Kamal could apologise to Vishal, read his messages, and give him a real task like the survey, judging him on new work.

qa.q: What has the past month been like for Vishal?
qa.a: Vishal has likely felt sidelined and frustrated, offering twice to help and being ignored because of one late summary.

grounding: A student admits aloud to deciding a groupmate was useless after one late submission and then giving him no tasks for a month.

passage:
Week 1, Friday. Devesh's slides arrived at 12:40 a.m., well past the 10 p.m. deadline Vidya had set. She typed in the group chat, "Noted," and in her own notebook wrote: Don't count on Devesh.
Week 3, Wednesday. Vidya shared the new task list. Survey, analysis, poster. Devesh's name was on none of them. When he asked, "Anything for me?" she replied, "It's fine, I've got it," and stayed up till two doing the analysis herself.
Week 5, Monday. The tutor asked each member to present their part. Devesh stood up with nothing to show and said, "I wasn't given anything after week one." The tutor looked at Vidya. Her face burned. On the walk out she caught up with him. "The conclusion section is yours. I'm sorry." He nodded slowly. "I was late once, Vidya."

qa.q: What did Vidya write in her notebook in week 1?
qa.a: Don't count on Devesh.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling when the tutor looked at her in week 5?
qa.a: Her face burned with embarrassment and guilt, because she saw that she had shut Devesh out over one late night.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could fix it?
qa.a: Vidya let one late submission define Devesh and stopped giving him tasks; giving him the conclusion section and judging his new work can fix it.

qa.q: How might Devesh see the weeks after that first deadline?
qa.a: Devesh probably felt pushed aside and frustrated, asking for work and getting none because of a single late upload.

grounding: Shows over several weeks a student deciding a groupmate is useless after one late submission and giving him no tasks.

passage: Mehak beta, you say your project partner is hopeless because he missed one deadline? Let me tell you about my engineering days in Roorkee. Our surveying group had four boys. One of them, Joginder, turned up late on the very first field day, and our readings started an hour behind. Your Raghav Nana, very sure of himself, decided that fellow was useless. For the whole term I gave him only the measuring chain to carry. Never the readings, never the drawings. Then in the final week I fell ill and could not finish the map. Joginder sat up two nights and drew it, cleaner than I ever could. He had been late that first day because the bus from his village broke down. I never asked. I lost a whole term of his help because of one hour.

qa.q: What was the only job Raghav Nana gave Joginder for the term?
qa.a: He gave him only the measuring chain to carry.

qa.q: What was young Raghav feeling when he decided Joginder was useless?
qa.a: He felt annoyed and very sure of himself, certain one late morning showed what kind of person Joginder was.

qa.q: Which moment in the story could have changed things much earlier?
qa.a: On the first field day, simply asking Joginder why he was late would have revealed the broken-down bus.

qa.q: How might Joginder have felt carrying only the chain all term?
qa.a: Joginder likely felt underused and quietly hurt, yet he still stepped in to draw the map when it mattered.

grounding: An elder recalls deciding a groupmate was useless after one late morning and giving him no real tasks for a whole term.

passage:
Monday. The client called at nine: the invoice Karthik sent had the wrong amount, by a lot. Amandeep apologised, fixed it, and by lunch had half-written an email moving Karthik off the account. She didn't send it. Something about how fast she'd written it bothered her.
Tuesday. She opened Karthik's work log for the whole year. Eleven months, forty-odd invoices, no errors. She also noticed the new billing tool had gone live last Thursday, and two other people had filed bug reports since.
Thursday. She sat with Karthik. "Walk me through Monday." He showed her the screen where the tool had pulled last year's rate. He had checked the total but not the rate line. "That part's on me," he said. Amandeep deleted the draft email. Instead they added a rate check to the team's list, and she asked the tool team to fix the bug.

qa.q: How many months of Karthik's work log showed no errors?
qa.a: Eleven months, with forty-odd invoices and no errors.

qa.q: Why didn't Amandeep send the email on Monday?
qa.a: She felt uneasy about how quickly she had written it, sensing that one error was colouring her whole view of Karthik.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Reviewing Karthik's full year and the new tool's bugs before deciding, which showed one slip in context rather than a pattern.

qa.q: How might Karthik have felt when asked to walk through Monday?
qa.a: Karthik was probably nervous but relieved to be asked, and he felt able to own his part honestly.

grounding: Shows a team lead noticing one mistake was colouring her view and reviewing the person's full record and context before deciding.

passage: Pallavi, you're about to sack that young cook for one bad dinner? Sit down and listen to your Rekha Mausi. When I was your age, I ran the kitchen at a hotel in Udaipur. One night, the biggest wedding order of the season, the dal came out burnt. Forty guests. I was shaking with anger at the boy on that stove. I had his dismissal letter half-typed. Then my old head chef said, "Rekha, look at his book first." We kept a book for every cook. His had two years of neat entries, praised twice by guests by name. And that night, I found out, the gas pressure had dropped and nobody had told him. I tore up the letter. I gave him a warning about tasting before serving, and we got the gas line fixed. That boy runs his own kitchen in Jaipur now.

qa.q: Where did Rekha run the kitchen at Pallavi's age?
qa.a: At a hotel in Udaipur.

qa.q: What was young Rekha feeling when she half-typed the dismissal letter?
qa.a: She was shaking with anger at the cook, with one burnt dish filling her whole view of him.

qa.q: Which choice in the story turned things around?
qa.a: Looking at the cook's book of two years' neat work and learning about the gas pressure drop before deciding.

qa.q: How did the cook's future change because of that choice?
qa.a: Instead of being sacked, he got a fair warning and a fixed gas line, and he later ran his own kitchen in Jaipur.

grounding: An elder recalls nearly firing a cook after one ruined dish and instead reviewing his full record and the context first.

passage: The client wanted a name for tomorrow's presentation by 6 p.m., and it was already 4:15. Tanuja's first thought was simple: not Dilnaz. Yesterday Dilnaz had sent a chart with the wrong axis label, and Tanuja had spotted it only minutes before it went out. The office was loud with a fire drill, alarms beeping, people filing past. Tanuja stood by the stairs and made herself do one thing: open the shared folder. Dilnaz had built nine of the team's last ten client decks. The comments from clients were warm. And yesterday, Tanuja remembered now, Dilnaz had been covering for someone on leave, doing two jobs at once. Tanuja felt her certainty loosen. At 5:40 she wrote: "Dilnaz presents. I'll do a second check on the charts tonight." Dilnaz replied with a single word: "Thanks."

qa.q: How many of the team's last ten client decks had Dilnaz built?
qa.a: Nine of the team's last ten client decks.

qa.q: How did Tanuja feel once she had looked at the shared folder?
qa.a: She felt her certainty loosen, as the full record and the double workload made the one error look like a slip, not the whole picture.

qa.q: What small step helped Tanuja decide fairly under time pressure?
qa.a: Opening the shared folder to check Dilnaz's full record, then adding a second check on the charts rather than dropping her.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz feel on being chosen after yesterday's mistake?
qa.a: Dilnaz probably feels relieved and trusted, since one error did not cancel out months of good work.

grounding: Shows a lead under time pressure noticing one error is colouring her view and checking the colleague's full record and context before deciding.

passage: The lunch bell rang and the corridor outside Class 3 filled in seconds. Suraj was carrying his water bottle with the lid open when Ramesh bumped into him. Water splashed all over Suraj's shirt. "You did that on purpose!" Suraj shouted. "Ramesh is mean. Everyone knows." Ramesh opened his mouth, but a wave of children pushed him away. Two minutes later, rushing to the canteen, Suraj knocked a small girl's tiffin out of her hands. "Sorry, sorry, it's so crowded!" he said, and kept going. The duty teacher had seen both. "Suraj, when you bumped her, why did it happen?" "Because of the crowd." "And when Ramesh bumped you?" Suraj stopped. He looked back at the corridor, packed from wall to wall.

qa.q: What did Suraj knock out of the small girl's hands?
qa.a: Her tiffin.

qa.q: Why did Suraj feel so sure Ramesh bumped him on purpose?
qa.a: Soaked and upset, Suraj felt angry and blamed Ramesh's character, without noticing the crowded corridor he later used as his own excuse.

qa.q: How did the duty teacher help Suraj see the pattern?
qa.a: The teacher asked the same question about both bumps, so Suraj could compare his reason for himself with his reason for Ramesh.

qa.q: What is it like for Ramesh to be called mean in front of everyone?
qa.a: Ramesh probably feels hurt and unfairly judged, and he couldn't even explain because the crowd pushed him away.

grounding: Shows a child calling another child mean for bumping him in a crowded corridor while excusing his own bump as the crowd's fault.

passage:
Monday. In the crush at the school-bus door, Leela stepped on Akash's new shoe. He glared all the way home and told Amma, "Leela is the rudest girl in the whole bus."
Wednesday. It rained, and everyone rushed for the bus at once. Akash, pushing to get a window seat, elbowed a younger boy into the door. The boy cried out. "It wasn't me, everyone was pushing!" Akash said.
Friday. Akash got on first for once and watched from the window. The queue was a tangle of umbrellas and bags. Leela was squeezed near the door, trying not to step on anyone, and still bumped a Class 2 boy. She looked so sorry. Akash thought about Monday. Maybe it hadn't been rude. Maybe it had just been the door.

qa.q: What did Leela step on at the school-bus door?
qa.a: Akash's new shoe.

qa.q: How did Akash feel about Leela after Monday?
qa.a: He felt angry and sure that she was simply rude, calling her the rudest girl in the whole bus.

qa.q: What could Akash do the next time someone bumps him?
qa.a: He could look at the situation first, like the crowded door, before deciding the person is rude.

qa.q: How might the younger boy Akash elbowed see Akash on Wednesday?
qa.a: The younger boy may think Akash is rough or mean, just as Akash had judged Leela.

grounding: Shows a child blaming a girl's character for a bump at a crowded bus door while excusing his own push as everyone pushing.

passage: Hrithik, stop sulking. You say that boy in your class shoved you because he's a bully? Let me tell you what happened to your Bhupen Dadu when I was about your size. It was the Rath Yatra fair in Puri, the crowd like a river. A boy in a yellow shirt knocked my sugar candy right into the mud. I decided he was the wickedest boy in Odisha. I told my mother and cousins. Then, ten minutes later, the crowd surged, and I fell against an old man and knocked his glasses off. I said, "It was the crowd, it wasn't me!" My mother just looked at me. "And the boy in yellow?" she asked. I had no answer. So, Hrithik, was the corridor crowded when he shoved you?

qa.q: What did the boy in the yellow shirt knock into the mud?
qa.a: Bhupen Dadu's sugar candy.

qa.q: What was young Bhupen feeling toward the boy in yellow?
qa.a: He felt angry and sure the boy was the wickedest boy in Odisha, judging his character instead of the crowd.

qa.q: Which moment in the story made young Bhupen rethink?
qa.a: When his mother asked "And the boy in yellow?" right after he blamed the crowd for knocking off the old man's glasses.

qa.q: How might the old man have seen young Bhupen's excuse?
qa.a: The old man might have accepted that the crowd was to blame, the same understanding Bhupen had refused the boy in yellow.

grounding: An elder recalls blaming a boy's character for a bump at a crowded fair while excusing his own bump as the crowd's fault.

passage: Devika, you've been checking that phone every two minutes. Your friend hasn't replied, and you've decided she doesn't care? Listen to your Hafsa Khala. When I was in Class 11, we had no phones, only letters and one landline in the lane. I wrote my best friend a long letter about a boy I liked, and a fight with my Abbu. Two weeks, no reply. Then she didn't come to my birthday. I told everyone she was selfish, that she had new friends now. I even tore up her photo. A month later her younger brother came to our door. Their mother had been in hospital all that time, and my friend was cooking, cleaning, sitting by the bed. My letter was still unopened on her table. I never forgot how quickly I decided who she was.

qa.q: What did Hafsa Khala tear up?
qa.a: Her friend's photo.

qa.q: What was young Hafsa feeling when her friend missed her birthday?
qa.a: She felt hurt and angry, and decided her friend was selfish and had new friends, without imagining what else might be happening.

qa.q: Which moment in the story could Hafsa have handled differently?
qa.a: When the letter went unanswered, she could have asked the friend's family if all was well instead of telling everyone her friend was selfish.

qa.q: What was that month like for the friend?
qa.a: The friend was busy cooking, cleaning and sitting by her mother's hospital bed, with no time even to open a letter.

grounding: An elder recalls deciding a friend who did not reply was uncaring when the friend was really caught up in a family crisis.

passage: 11:05 p.m., the night before the chemistry exam. Kalyani had sent Rajni four messages asking for the photos of the organic notes. Two grey ticks, never blue. "Wow," Kalyani muttered. "She's online all day, but for me, nothing." She had no notes for three chapters and less than eight hours before the exam. She wrote a fifth message and deleted it, then wrote, "Thanks for nothing." Her finger shook over send. Instead she tried the class group, and a boy she barely knew sent the photos at midnight. In the morning, at the school gate, Rajni ran up, hair wet, eyes red. "Our whole building had no power last night. My phone died at nine. I charged it in the bus just now and saw your messages." Kalyani felt her face go hot. The deleted message was still in her head.

qa.q: How many messages had Kalyani sent Rajni by 11:05 p.m.?
qa.a: Four messages asking for the photos of the organic notes.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling when she typed "Thanks for nothing"?
qa.a: She felt hurt and angry, sure that Rajni was ignoring her on purpose while being online all day.

qa.q: What helped Kalyani avoid making things worse, and what could she try next time?
qa.a: Not sending the message and asking the class group helped; next time she could think of dead phones or power cuts before deciding a friend doesn't care.

qa.q: How might Rajni have felt if the "Thanks for nothing" message had been waiting for her?
qa.a: Rajni would likely have felt hurt and unfairly accused, since her phone had died in a power cut.

grounding: Shows a teenager, under exam pressure, deciding a friend who did not reply is uncaring when the friend's phone had simply died.

passage: Vikas saw Tanvir coming out of the stationery shop near the Sector 15 market and waved hard. Tanvir looked straight through him and walked on, fast, head down. Vikas felt his cheeks burn. They had sat together all year. That evening he told his cousin, "Tanvir's become so full of himself since he made the football team. Didn't even say hi." He left Tanvir out of the group chat plan for Sunday's movie. On Monday Tanvir wasn't in school. On Tuesday he came in quiet and pale, and at lunch he said, "Sorry about Saturday. I'd just got a call that my Nani had collapsed. I was running to the auto stand." Vikas stared at his lunchbox. He had built a whole story about Tanvir from one walk past.

qa.q: Where did Vikas see Tanvir on Saturday?
qa.a: Coming out of the stationery shop near the Sector 15 market.

qa.q: What was Vikas feeling when Tanvir walked past without a word?
qa.a: Vikas felt embarrassed and snubbed, his cheeks burning, and quickly decided Tanvir had become full of himself.

qa.q: What could Vikas do before judging a friend who seems rude?
qa.a: He could ask the friend if everything is all right, or wait to hear more, before deciding it is about their character.

qa.q: What was Saturday like for Tanvir?
qa.a: Tanvir had just heard his Nani had collapsed and was rushing to the auto stand, too frightened to notice anyone waving.

grounding: Shows a teenager deciding a friend who ignored him is arrogant when the friend was rushing to a family emergency.

passage: The group project for Urban Planning met every Tuesday at nine in the Manchester university library, and every Tuesday Wei was late or yawning. By week four Kwame had had enough. "He's just lazy," he told the other two. "He does the bare minimum and sleeps through meetings." He started writing Wei's sections himself. Then one Friday at six in the morning, Kwame went to the big supermarket near the station for milk. At the loading bay, in a grey uniform, stacking crates onto a trolley, was Wei. He looked exhausted. He saw Kwame and gave a small, awkward wave. "Night shift," Wei said. "Five nights a week. My rent." Kwame stood holding his milk and thought of every Tuesday he had called him lazy.

qa.q: What was Wei doing at the supermarket loading bay?
qa.a: Stacking crates onto a trolley, in a grey uniform.

qa.q: Why did Kwame feel so sure Wei was lazy?
qa.a: Kwame felt frustrated by the late arrivals and yawns, and with no idea of Wei's nights, a personal flaw seemed the only explanation.

qa.q: What could Kwame do now in the group?
qa.a: He could apologise, ask Wei what meeting times work, and share tasks in a way that fits the night shifts.

qa.q: What have the Tuesday meetings been like for Wei?
qa.a: Wei probably felt drained and judged, arriving straight from night shifts while the group thought he didn't care.

grounding: Shows a student calling a groupmate lazy before discovering he works night shifts to pay his rent.

passage: The hostel warden at the Bhopal engineering college had put Sachin and Nitin in Room 214 in August. By October Sachin had decided his roommate was hopeless. Nitin slept until noon, missed the morning lab-group meetings, and left his half of the room a mess of uniforms and energy-bar wrappers. "Some people just don't care," Sachin said loudly in the mess one day. Then, one night, Sachin woke at two to find Nitin's bed empty. At seven Nitin came in, dropped a headset on the desk and fell asleep in his clothes. The headset had a sticker from a call centre on the ring road. Sachin looked at the uniforms on the chair again. Same logo. He sat on his bed for a long time, the mess-hall comment ringing in his ears.

qa.q: What sticker did Sachin see on Nitin's headset?
qa.a: A sticker from a call centre on the ring road.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling as he sat on his bed at the end?
qa.a: He felt uncomfortable and guilty, remembering the loud mess-hall comment he made about Nitin not caring.

qa.q: How could Sachin support Nitin in their lab group now?
qa.a: He could talk to Nitin privately and suggest the group move meetings to times that fit Nitin's night shifts.

qa.q: What would change if the lab group knew about Nitin's job?
qa.a: They would likely see his missed mornings as tiredness from working nights, not laziness, and plan around it.

grounding: Shows a student judging his roommate as lazy and careless without knowing he works night shifts at a call centre.

passage:
Dear Professor Vasudha,
I am writing about our group for the transport project. I think Dev should be moved to another group, or at least marked separately.
He has missed three of our five morning meetings. When he does come, he is usually yawning and once smelled strongly of bread and ovens, like he hadn't even gone home. He keeps asking if we can meet after 2 p.m., which doesn't suit anyone. His sections are short, though I admit they are accurate.
I have tried to be patient. But honestly, some people just don't take university seriously, and it isn't fair on the rest of us.
Could we discuss this in your office hours on Thursday?
Regards,
Yusuf

qa.q: How many of the five morning meetings has Dev missed?
qa.a: He has missed three of our five morning meetings.

qa.q: What is Yusuf feeling while writing the email?
qa.a: Yusuf feels frustrated and resentful, sure that Dev simply doesn't take university seriously.

qa.q: What would you advise Yusuf before sending this email?
qa.a: Ask Dev directly why mornings are hard, since the bread smell and afternoon requests hint at something like early or night work.

qa.q: How might Dev see Yusuf's request to move him?
qa.a: Dev might feel hurt and misjudged if he is working hard somewhere else and still turning in accurate sections.

grounding: A student's email calls a groupmate lazy while overlooking clues that he may be working nights at a bakery.

passage:
Wednesday, late.
Hrithik missed the supplier call again today. Third time this month. My first thought, honestly, was: he's careless, and I'm tired of covering for him. I even started typing that to our manager. Then I stopped. Hrithik has never been like this before March. So what changed in March? I don't know. Maybe something at home, maybe the new commute, maybe he really is just slipping. It could be both. Tomorrow I'll ask him, just him, over tea: "Is something making mornings hard?" If there's a reason, we'll sort the call times. If there isn't, I'll tell him plainly that the calls matter. Either way I'd rather ask than guess.
Dolma

qa.q: How many times has Hrithik missed the supplier call this month?
qa.a: Third time this month.

qa.q: What does Dolma feel at first about Hrithik missing the call?
qa.a: Dolma feels tired and irritated, thinking Hrithik is careless and not wanting to keep covering for him.

qa.q: What is Dolma's plan, and why is it balanced?
qa.a: To ask Hrithik privately over tea what makes mornings hard, while still telling him plainly that calls matter if there is no reason.

qa.q: How might Hrithik feel being asked over tea rather than reported?
qa.a: Hrithik would likely feel respected and relieved, with a chance to explain before being judged.

grounding: A colleague's diary shows Dolma asking what might be happening for a coworker before calling him careless, open to both situation and habit.

passage: At the cooperative bank branch in Sirsi, Jaya noticed it on Friday: three passbook entries in Siddharth's hand, each with a digit wrong. A farmer had come back, upset. Jaya felt the old irritation rise. She had seen junior clerks turn sloppy before. Instead of scolding him at the counter, she waited until the shutters came down and pulled a stool beside his desk. "Your entries are usually clean. What's been different this week?" Siddharth hesitated. "The tube light over my counter is flickering since Monday. I've been squinting. And I've been rushing to catch the last bus." Jaya looked up; the light was flickering right then. "Light, we can fix tomorrow," she said. "Rushing, that's yours." He nodded. On Monday a new tube light went up, and Jaya checked his first ten entries herself.

qa.q: How many passbook entries had a digit wrong?
qa.a: Three passbook entries in Siddharth's hand, each with a digit wrong.

qa.q: Why did Jaya wait until the shutters came down to speak to Siddharth?
qa.a: She felt irritated but wanted to understand first, and waiting let her ask calmly instead of scolding him in front of customers.

qa.q: What balance did Jaya strike in her response?
qa.a: She fixed the flickering light, the situation, and still named his rushing as his to change, then checked his next entries herself.

qa.q: How might Siddharth feel about being asked rather than blamed?
qa.a: Siddharth probably felt relieved and fairly treated, able to admit his rushing because he wasn't attacked.

grounding: Shows a mature officer asking what might be behind a junior's errors before calling him careless, and finding both a situation and a habit.

passage: My name is Pankaj, and this is about carrom with Ganga didi. Last summer, when I won, I always said, "See? I'm the best striker in the building." When I lost, it was different. "The board is tilted." "You distracted me." Once I threw the striker on the sofa, calling it unlucky. Ganga didi never argued. One evening she said, "Come here, chhote bhai," and wrote two lists on the back of a calendar: "Why Pankaj wins" and "Why Pankaj loses." Under wins, she wrote what I said: my skill. Under losses: board, striker, didi. She showed it to me without a word. It looked so silly I laughed. Then I felt a little ashamed. I still say "board is tilted" sometimes. But now I hear it.

qa.q: What did Ganga didi write the two lists on?
qa.a: On the back of a calendar.

qa.q: What did Pankaj feel when he saw the two lists?
qa.a: He first laughed at how silly it looked, then felt a little ashamed, seeing he claimed every win but blamed everything else for losses.

qa.q: What did Ganga didi's lists help Pankaj notice, and what could he try now?
qa.a: They showed him he credits himself for wins and outside things for losses; he could now name one thing he did wrong when he loses.

qa.q: How might Ganga didi have felt hearing all those excuses?
qa.a: She was probably amused but also a bit tired of being blamed, so she chose a quiet, clear way to show him.

grounding: A child looks back on crediting his carrom wins to skill and blaming his losses on the board, the powder and his sister.

passage:
Badminton coaching, under-11 group, Saturday. Coach's note.
Madhav won both his morning games against Avni and told the group, "That's my smash. Nobody can return it." In the afternoon he lost twice to her. First he said the shuttle was bent. Then that the net was higher on his side. Then that I had called a line wrong. I had. Once. He was also double-hitting and not moving his feet, which is why he lost.
After the session I asked him two questions: "What made you win this morning?" "My smash." "What made you lose this afternoon?" He began to list the shuttle and the net, then stopped, and said, "Maybe my feet." Next week I will ask every child both questions after every game, so it becomes a habit.

qa.q: What did Madhav blame first for his afternoon loss?
qa.a: He said the shuttle was bent.

qa.q: Why did Madhav say "Maybe my feet"?
qa.a: Once asked both questions side by side, he seemed to feel less defensive and could see he was blaming outside things for losses but crediting himself for wins.

qa.q: What is the coach's plan, and why might it help?
qa.a: To ask every child both questions after every game, so looking at their own part in wins and losses becomes a habit.

qa.q: How might Avni feel when Madhav blames the shuttle and the net?
qa.a: Avni might feel her win is being taken away from her, as if she didn't earn it.

grounding: A coach's note shows a boy crediting wins to his smash and blaming losses on the shuttle, the net and the umpire.

passage:
Monday, week 1. The history unit test came back: 18 out of 20. Kashish grinned at her desk. "I'm just good at history," she told Hemant. She had revised for two evenings.
Friday, week 3. The geography test: 9 out of 20. "The questions were so unfair," Kashish said in the bus. "And ma'am never taught the map part properly. Plus it was so hot in the room." Hemant pointed out that he had got 15. She shrugged. "Lucky."
Sunday, week 4. Filling her study planner, Kashish saw the two weeks side by side. History: two evenings of revision. Geography: none; she had gone to her cousin's engagement. She sat back, pen in her mouth. "So... it wasn't ma'am," she said out loud to nobody. Then she blocked two evenings for geography.

qa.q: What did Kashish score in the history unit test?
qa.a: 18 out of 20.

qa.q: How did Kashish feel about her geography mark in week 3?
qa.a: She felt defensive and annoyed, blaming the questions, the teacher and the heat rather than her lack of revision.

qa.q: What small step helped Kashish see the truth, and how could she keep using it?
qa.a: Looking at her study planner for both weeks side by side; she could check it after every test before crediting or blaming anyone.

qa.q: How might Hemant see Kashish calling his 15 "lucky"?
qa.a: Hemant may feel his effort was brushed off, since she credits her own good marks to skill but his to luck.

grounding: Shows a teenager crediting a high mark to her talent and blaming a low one on the paper, the teacher and the heat.

passage: Tenzin, you've been blaming the examiner since you walked in. Come, sit with Arnab uncle on the balcony. In my second year of college in Darjeeling, I got top marks in English. I told everyone, even the bus conductor, that I was a born writer. Same term, I failed accounts. I told everyone the paper was set by a madman, the hall was freezing, my pen was leaking. My father listened, said nothing, and the next morning put my two notebooks on the table. English: full, every page, notes in the margin. Accounts: six pages, and then doodles of football players. I was so angry at him for that. For a week I didn't speak to him. And then I opened the accounts book again, from page seven.

qa.q: Where did Arnab uncle go to college?
qa.a: In Darjeeling.

qa.q: What was young Arnab feeling when his father put the notebooks on the table?
qa.a: He felt angry and exposed, because the notebooks showed his failure came from not studying, not from a mad paper.

qa.q: Which moment in the story was the turning point?
qa.a: When young Arnab finally opened the accounts book again from page seven, taking the low mark as his own to fix.

qa.q: How might Arnab's father have felt during the week of silence?
qa.a: He was probably hurt but patient, trusting that his son would come round once his pride settled.

grounding: An elder recalls crediting a top English mark to his talent and blaming a failed accounts paper on the examiner and the hall.
